benchmarks.note: Land benchmarks: average transacted ¥/tsubo by station, MLIT transaction data via Utinokati (multi-year unless noted): Tachikawa ~150 (545 deals; the station average mixes commercial plots, so residential streets sit below it — and a headline '2026 = 308' print rests on exactly one deal and is ignored), Yagawa ~97 (FY2024), Nishi-Tachikawa ~82 (multi-year only: single years swing from 65 to 115 on a handful of deals), Higashi-Nakagami ~79, Tamagawa-Josui ~71 (transactions and official-price estimates agree), Musashi-Sunagawa ~65, Seibu-Tachikawa scored at ~58: the raw transaction average (51) is dragged down by very large fringe lots, while the Ichiban-cho district official average is ~63. Nishi-Kunitachi is scored at ~120, NOT its thin transaction prints (~160 on 2–9 deals a year, station-front skewed): Hagoromo-cho's official residential points average ~107 and the listings here are 7–8 minutes out in low-rise streets. Sunagawa-Nanaban (~85), Shibasaki-Taiikukan (~115), Tappi (~95) and Izumi-Taiikukan (~80) are proxies from official district land-price points (Saiwai-cho ~91, Kashiwa-cho ~96, Sakae-cho ~96; Shibasaki-cho's all-use average of ~226 is commercial-inflated and not used) and neighbouring-station transactions, flagged as such. Walk bands apply Tachikawa's steep observed gradient — prices fall roughly 52% between the station front and a 10-minute walk at Tachikawa station. Used houses transacted at about ¥152万/tsubo city-wide (floor-area basis): Akebono-cho ~184, Kashiwa-cho ~178, Fujimi-cho ~160 at the top; the Sunagawa districts ~119–133. Official residential land prices rose +7.0% in the 2026 survey — five consecutive rises, accelerating (+1.1% in 2022 to +7.0% in 2026).
